hotspot_comment: The main cereal season has ended in the country and agricultural production is likely to be below average at the national level due to a very dry and poorly distributed October to May rainy season. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/502398a7] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for crops and the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/2f099317] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for rangelands point to a moderate probability of drier-than-normal conditions across many coastal and southern parts of the country for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. These forecasts are generally in line with expectations linked to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365] upcoming El Nino but will need to be monitored closely over the next months.

Harvest of season B crops is complete for beans and ongoing for sorghum and maize, while the country experienced in-average rainfall during the last 30 days. Below average biomass areas are recorded particularly in the west and in the north. In Bujumbura, 36% of the active cropland is in poor vegetation status. Despite pockets of below-average biomass, Gitega, which accounts for 11.7% of national cereal production, showed average biomass conditions throughout Season B. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/burundi/rapport-d-valuation-des-recoltes-des-approvisionnements-alimentaires-pour-la-saison] FEWSNET, the 2026B harvest will be cumulatively below-average in the semi-arid regions of the country (Imbo Plains, Northern Lowlands, and Eastern Lowlands), but cumulatively near-average nationally due to tubers and perennial crops balancing out large losses of beans.
Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

Vegetation conditions across much of Kenya deteriorated compared to June, reflecting the cumulative effects of below-average rainfall since late May and throughout June and July. The resulting moisture deficits are likely to have adversely affected pasture resources, particularly in the arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs). In the unimodal cropping zones, below-average rainfall slowed crop development and reduced soil moisture availability during critical crop growth stages. The impacts of the prolonged dry conditions are already evident across parts of western Kenya, including Kakamega, Bungoma, Uasin Gishu, Elgeyo Marakwet, and Trans Nzoia counties, among others. In several of the North Rift cereal-producing areas, prolonged moisture stress has resulted in irreversible crop wilting, with some maize fields unlikely to recover before harvest. [https://nation.africa/kenya/news/erratic-weather-puts-kenya-s-breadbasket-on-edge-5497196#story] Media reports and official government statements indicate that the prolonged July dry spell is already affecting crop production in several of Kenya's major cereal-producing counties with localized yield losses estimated at up to 60%. Looking ahead, forecasts of a strong El Niño for the upcoming short rains season point to an increased risk of adverse impacts including increased risk of flooding and other weather-related hazards. These conditions could further affect agricultural production, disrupt livelihoods, and complicate recovery efforts in areas already impacted by the current dry spell.

The main cereal season has ended in the country, with a varying regional performance: favourable rains benefitted crop development in the Northern Lowlands and Foothills leading to an above-average harvest, while late-season flooding caused widespread crop damage and below-average yields in the Southern Lowlands and Senqu River Valley ([https://fews.net/southern-africa/lesotho/food-security-outlook/june-2026] FEWSNET, June 2026). The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/502398a7] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for crops and the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/2f099317] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for rangelands point to a moderate probability of drier-than-normal conditions across the country for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. These forecasts are generally in line with expectations linked to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365] upcoming El Nino but will need to be monitored closely over the next months.

In Madagascar, harvest of rice and maize in the northern and central areas finalized in June with an overall output estimated close to average due to mixed crop conditions: above average crop biomass in Alaotra Mangoro, close to average in Vakinankaratra, Itasy and Analamanga, slightly below average in Sofia (possibly due to cyclone Fitya at end of January). The rice season started in November with good rainfall till December-January, then rainfall conditions shifted to below average levels in February in the centre north (from Analamanga to Sofia and Diana) and particularly in March in the central Highlands (from Haute Matsiatra to Alaotra Mangoro), and to a lower extent in April in Vakinankaratra and Bongolava in the central highlands, at the start of harvest.In the Grand South, below average rainfall since early February, combined with about 2C above average temperatures from February to May accelerated crop senescence and resulted in below average output of cereals and legume crops, especially in Anosy and Androy. The region is projected to have about 1.5 to 2.0 million people in acute food insecurity (IPC phase 3 and above) as a result of previous droughts (2020, 2021 and 2022), cyclones, poor socio economic conditions and aid reduction, according to the latest [https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1161004/?iso3=MDG] IPC analysis and [https://reliefweb.int/report/madagascar/madagascar-food-security-outlook-early-lean-season-and-el-nino-challenge-food-security-grand-south-june-2026-january-2027] FEWS-NET.

The main cereal season has ended in the country, with average yields according to [https://fews.net/southern-africa/malawi/food-security-outlook/june-2026] FEWS NET (June 2026), however, dry spells and flooding caused below-average harvests in southern livelihood zones (Southern Lakeshore, Middle Shire, and Lower Shire).

The main cereal season has ended in the country, and the cereal output is expected to be above the five-year average ([https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/e489e61d-122b-4332-b18a-6005828dee46] FAO, Crop Prospects and Food Situation (July 2026)). According to preliminary data from the Namibian Agronomic Board the white maize production is forecast at 111,447 tonnes, representing a significant 37% increase compared to last year's harvest ([https://www.nbcnews.na/node/116305] NBC News). Additionally, the favourable weather has significantly improved rangelands, which is set to boost livestock production. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/502398a7] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for crops and the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/2f099317] JRC ASAP forecast warnings for rangelands point to a moderate probability of drier-than-normal conditions across many parts of country for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. These forecasts are generally in line with expectations linked to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365] upcoming El Nino but will need to be monitored closely over the next months.

Season B harvest is complete for beans and ongoing for sorghum and maize. While precipitation has been recorded in-average during the last 30 days, biomass indicators are below average particularly [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/f6bbac73] in the east of the country. In Kirehe, accounting for the 7% of the national cereal production, 42% of the active cropland is seen in poor vegetation status. ASAP end of season biomass warnings are present in 13 districts. The latest [https://openknowledge.fao.org/items/e489e61d-122b-4332-b18a-6005828dee46] Crop Prospects and Food Situation report confirms that, in Rwanda, uneven seasonal rainfall patterns are expected to constrain yields of the 2026B harvests. [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service point to dry outlook until September, with a sudden shift to wet from October, in agreement with the expected influence of ongoing El Niño conditions.

Harvest is underway for Msimu crops in unimodal areas (sorghum, rice, and maize) and Masika crops in bimodal areas (sorghum, millet, and maize). Precipitation has been recorded in average during the last 30 days. Biomass is now in average throughout the country with the exception of Morogoro, Pwani and Tanga, which suffer from previous lack of rainfall. In Dodoma, the country's top cereal-producing region, biomass is recorded above average (+10%). According to [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=TZA] FAO/GIEWS, aggregate cereal production in 2026 is tentatively forecast at near-average levels of 12.8 million tonnes, despite localized production shortfalls caused by erratic seasonal rains and prolonged dry spells, compounded by low fertilizer application rates linked to post-election port disruptions and rising international input prices; about 507,000 people (5 percent of the analysed population) are projected to face severe acute food insecurity between June 2026 and January 2027. [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service point to dry outlook until September, particuralrly in the north, followed by a sudden shift to wet from October, in agreement with the expected influence of ongoing El Niño conditions.

The first cropping season has ended across the bimodal areas of central and southern Uganda, with mixed production outcomes expected. Agro-climatic conditions were generally favourable during the onset of the season from February through March, supporting timely planting and good crop establishment. However, the uneven distribution of rainfall during April, May, and June, followed by prolonged dry spells in several areas, likely constrained crop development during the critical stages. IPC estimates for the current period (April – July 2026) In Karamoja region show that 473,000 people are in IPC Phase 3 or above) including 41,000 people in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency) and 432,000 in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis).

The main cereal season has ended in the country and according to the [https://www.agriculture.gov.zm/2026/05/zambia-projected-to-produce-nearly-5-million-metric-tonnes-of-maize/] Ministry of Agriculture of Zambia, the maize harvest is projected at 4,937,605 metric tonnes, making it the highest maize production ever recorded in the country’s history. These forecasts are generally in line with expectations linked to the [https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147365] upcoming El Nino but will need to be monitored closely over the next months.
